claims.text: Factorisation is the opposite process of expanding brackets.
claims.quote: Factorisation is the opposite process of expanding brackets.

claims.text: Factorisation starts with the expanded expression and ends with a bracketed one; for example, start with 2x+2 and end up with 2(x+1).
claims.quote: Factorisation would be to start with $2x+2$ and end up with $2(x+1)$

claims.text: The expressions 2(x+1) and 2x+2 are equivalent: they have the same value for all values of x.
claims.quote: The two expressions $2(x+1)$ and $2x+2$ are equivalent; they have the same value for all values of $x$

claims.text: Factorising based on common factors relies on there being factors common to all the terms.
claims.quote: Factorising based on common factors relies on there being factors common to all the terms.

claims.text: The expression 2x - 6x^2 can be factorised as 2x(1 - 3x).
The taking out of common factors is the starting point in all factorisation problems.
claims.quote: The taking out of common factors is the starting point in all factorisation problems.

claims.text: The expression 2(x - 1) - a(x - 1) can be factorised as (x - 1)(2 - a).
A "switch around" strategy is used to find the common factor when the brackets, such as (a - 2) and (2 - a), differ in sign.
claims.quote: strategy to find the common factor

claims.text: 2 - a = -(a - 2): switching the terms in a bracket gives the negative of the original bracket.
Writing 2 - a as -(a - 2), the expression 5(a - 2) - b(2 - a) becomes 5(a - 2) - [-b(a - 2)], which equals 5(a - 2) + b(a - 2).
Taking out the common factor (a - 2) from 5(a - 2) + b(a - 2) gives (a - 2)(5 + b).
(ax + b)(ax - b) can be expanded to a^2x^2 - b^2.
a^2x^2 - b^2 can be factorised as (ax + b)(ax - b).
x^2 - 16 can be written as x^2 - 4^2, which is a difference of two squares.
claims.quote: ${x}^{2}-16$ can be written as ${x}^{2}-{4}^{2}$ which is a difference of two squares

claims.text: The factors of x^2 - 16 are (x - 4) and (x + 4).
To spot a difference of two squares, look for an expression consisting of two terms.
To spot a difference of two squares, look for terms that have different signs (one positive, one negative).
claims.quote: with terms that have different signs (one positive, one negative)

claims.text: To spot a difference of two squares, look for each term being a perfect square.
claims.quote: with each term a perfect square

claims.text: Examples of a difference of two squares are a^2 - 1, 4x^2 - y^2 and -49 + p^4.
Take out the common factor (a^2 - 4) from 3a(a^2 - 4) - 7(a^2 - 4) to get (a^2 - 4)(3a - 7).
Then factorise the difference of two squares: (a^2 - 4)(3a - 7) = (a - 2)(a + 2)(3a - 7).
The factors of 3x + 3 are 3 and (x + 1).
The factors of 2x^2 + 2x are 2x and (x + 1).
The expression 2x^2 + 2x + 3x + 3 has no common factor to all four terms, but it can still be factorised by grouping the terms.
claims.quote: there is no common factor to all four terms, but we can factorise as follows

claims.text: Group the terms in pairs and take out the common factor of each pair: (2x^2 + 2x) + (3x + 3) = 2x(x + 1) + 3(x + 1).
After taking out the common factor from each pair, there is another common factor, (x + 1).
Taking out the common factor (x + 1) gives (x + 1)(2x + 3).
To get the second factor, take out the common bracket (x + 1) and see what is left over.
claims.quote: We get this by taking out the $\left(x+1\right)$ and seeing what is left over

claims.text: What is left over is 2x from the first group and +3 from the second group.
claims.quote: We have $2x$ from the first group and $\text{+3}$ from the second group

claims.text: Factorising a four-term expression by grouping the terms in pairs and taking out the common bracket is called factorising by grouping.
claims.quote: This is called factorising by grouping.

claims.text: In 7x + 14y + bx + 2by, the ratio of the coefficients 7:14 is the same as b:2b, so 7 is a common factor of the first two terms and b is a common factor of the second two terms.
claims.quote: We see that the ratio of the coefficients $7:14$ is the same as $b:2b$

claims.text: Group terms with common factors together: 7x + 14y + bx + 2by = (7x + 14y) + (bx + 2by) = 7(x + 2y) + b(x + 2y).
claims.quote: Group terms with common factors together: $\text{7}$ is a common factor of the first two terms and $b$ is a common factor of the second two terms

claims.text: Take out the common factor (x + 2y): 7(x + 2y) + b(x + 2y) = (x + 2y)(7 + b).
Alternatively, group x as the common factor of the first and third terms and 2y as the common factor of the second and fourth terms, where 7:b = 14:2b.

claims.text: Rearrange the equation with grouped terms together: 7x + 14y + bx + 2by = (7x + bx) + (14y + 2by) = x(7 + b) + 2y(7 + b).
claims.quote: Rearrange the equation with grouped terms together

claims.text: Take out the common factor (7 + b): x(7 + b) + 2y(7 + b) = (7 + b)(x + 2y).
The factors of 7x + 14y + bx + 2by are (7 + b) and (x + 2y).

solution: Use a “switch around” strategy to find the common factor. Notice that $2-a=-(a-2)$ $\begin{align*}5(a-2)-b(2-a)&=5(a-2)-[-b(a-2)]\\&=5(a-2)+b(a-2)\\&=(a-2)(5+b)\end{align*}$
Factorise the difference of two squares $({a}^{2}-4)$: $({a}^{2}-4)(3a-7)=(a-2)(a+2)(3a-7)$

solution: Group terms with common factors together: $\text{7}$ is a common factor of the first two terms and $b$ is a common factor of the second two terms. We see that the ratio of the coefficients $7:14$ is the same as $b:2b$ . $\begin{align*}7x+14y+bx+2by&=\left(7x+14y\right)+\left(bx+2by\right)\\&=7\left(x+2y\right)+b\left(x+2y\right)\end{align*}$
Take out the common factor $\left(x+2y\right)$: $7\left(x+2y\right)+b\left(x+2y\right)=\left(x+2y\right)\left(7+b\right)$ OR
Group terms with common factors together: $x$ is a common factor of the first and third terms and $2y$ is a common factor of the second and fourth terms $\left(7:b=14:2b\right)$ .
Rearrange the equation with grouped terms together: $\begin{align*}7x+14y+bx+2by&=\left(7x+bx\right)+\left(14y+2by\right)\\&=x\left(7+b\right)+2y\left(7+b\right)\end{align*}$
Write the final answer: The factors of $7x+14y+bx+2by$ are $\left(7+b\right)$ and $\left(x+2y\right)$ .
